sections.content: How many people stayed in Grays after gaining qualifications?

Grays is a medium-sized town in the East of England. Grays does not have its own university.

Grays has medium levels of deprivation.

Overall, Grays ended up with:

  • a similar number of graduates as it produced
  • a similar number of non-graduates with advanced qualifications as it produced
Note: all towns and cities in this analysis are defined based on population size only. This means that some cities are classed as towns because of their population.

Let's explore this further

There were 3,080 state-school pupils from Grays who sat their GCSEs between the 2007 to 2008 and the 2010 to 2011 school years.

Of these, 880 (29%) went on to gain degree-level qualifications (level 6+ as defined by The Office of Qualifications and Examinations Regulation, or Ofqual ). We will call these people graduates.

Another 1,020 (33%) went on to gain other advanced post-16 qualifications, such as A-Levels, a foundation degree or higher apprenticeship (levels 3-5 as defined by Ofqual). In this tool, we will refer to these non-graduates with advanced qualifications as “qualified non-graduates", for brevity.

The charts below compare Grays to other English towns and cities using three measures:

  • what proportion of Grays' pupils became graduates or qualified non-graduates by the 2017 to 2018 academic year
  • of those graduates and qualified non-graduates, the percentages that lived in Grays in the 2018 to 2019 academic year
  • how many graduates and qualified non-graduates from elsewhere came to live there by 2018 to 2019, relative to the number who sat their GCSEs there

In some towns, some of this information may not be available because of small sample sizes.
The size and deprivation level of a town, as well as the qualification levels of older residents, were all related to students' educational attainment. Read our previous analysis.

Where did those who left Grays move to?

Of Grays's graduates, 285 were living elsewhere in 2018/19.

However, 100 of those graduates (35%) were living fairly locally, in the London travel to work area (TTWA).

Of Grays's qualified (level 3+) non-graduates, 305 were living elsewhere in 2018/19.

However, 105 of those qualified non-graduates (34%) were living fairly locally, in the London travel to work area (TTWA).

Of those in Grays' GCSE cohort:

  • 175 graduates left the East of England
  • the most common region they moved to was London
  • 115 qualified (level 3+) non-graduates left the East of England
  • the most common region they moved to was London

In 2018 to 2019, 28% of graduates and 30% of qualified non-graduates living in Grays had moved there from elsewhere

In the 2018 to 2019 academic year, there were 805 graduates and 1,005 qualified (level 3+) non-graduates from our cohort living in Grays. This is compared with the 880 graduates and 1,020 qualified non-graduates who had lived there when they sat their GCSEs.

In 2018 to 2019, 72% of the graduates had also lived in Grays as GCSE pupils, while 28% had moved there from elsewhere.

Of the qualified non-graduates who lived in Grays in 2018 to 2019, 70% had lived there as GCSE pupils, while 30% had moved to the area from elsewhere.
